claim: The RTs during error trials fell in the middle of the distributions of correct RTs, neither consistently fast nor consistently slow.
source: Also note that, compared to those of correct saccades, the RTs of incorrect saccades were neither consistently fast, as might be expected on the basis of strong anticipation, nor consistently slow, as might be expected from a protracted deliberation process (Figure 2e). Instead, the RTs during errors fell squarely in the middle of the distributions of correct RTs (for correct trials, 90% of RTs were inside the ranges 158–432 ms and 146–404 ms for monkeys G and K, respectively; for errors, the ranges were 180–336 and 152–388 ms).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific RT ranges for correct and error trials, and Figure 2e shows the distributions.

claim: For correct trials, 90% of RTs were inside the range 158–432 ms for monkey G.
source: Instead, the RTs during errors fell squarely in the middle of the distributions of correct RTs (for correct trials, 90% of RTs were inside the ranges 158–432 ms and 146–404 ms for monkeys G and K, respectively; for errors, the ranges were 180–336 and 152–388 ms).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific RT range measurements from experimental data.

claim: For correct trials, 90% of RTs were inside the range 146–404 ms for monkey K.
source: Instead, the RTs during errors fell squarely in the middle of the distributions of correct RTs (for correct trials, 90% of RTs were inside the ranges 158–432 ms and 146–404 ms for monkeys G and K, respectively; for errors, the ranges were 180–336 and 152–388 ms).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific RT range measurements from experimental data.

claim: For error trials, 90% of RTs were inside the range 180–336 ms for monkey G.
source: Instead, the RTs during errors fell squarely in the middle of the distributions of correct RTs (for correct trials, 90% of RTs were inside the ranges 158–432 ms and 146–404 ms for monkeys G and K, respectively; for errors, the ranges were 180–336 and 152–388 ms).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific RT range measurements from experimental data.

claim: For error trials, 90% of RTs were inside the range 152–388 ms for monkey K.
source: Instead, the RTs during errors fell squarely in the middle of the distributions of correct RTs (for correct trials, 90% of RTs were inside the ranges 158–432 ms and 146–404 ms for monkeys G and K, respectively; for errors, the ranges were 180–336 and 152–388 ms).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific RT range measurements from experimental data.

claim: 132 FEF neurons were recorded from two monkeys (67 in monkey G; 65 in monkey K).
source: We recorded single-unit activity from 132 FEF neurons in the two monkeys (67 in monkey G; 65 in monkey K) during performance of the 1DR task.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of neurons recorded from each monkey.

claim: The rise-to-threshold process is the key building block of virtually all models of decision-making in which multiple-choice alternatives are evaluated over time.
source: This rise-to-threshold process is of enormous conceptual importance, as it is the key building block of virtually all models of decision-making in which multiple-choice alternatives, typically guided by perceptual information, are evaluated over time (Gold and Shadlen, 2001; Erlhagen and Schöner, 2002; Smith and Ratcliff, 2004; Brown and Heathcote, 2008; Stanford et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Thura et al., 2012; Brunton et al., 2013; Miller and Katz, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that use the rise-to-threshold process in decision-making models.

claim: Neurons that encode motor plans seem to reach a consistent firing level just before the onset of a saccade, particularly in the superior colliculus (SC) and the frontal eye field (FEF).
source: Notably, neurons that encode motor plans seem to reach a consistent firing level just before the onset of a saccade, particularly in the superior colliculus (SC) and the frontal eye field (FEF) (Hanes and Schall, 1996; Brown et al., 2008; Stanford et al., 2010; Ding and Gold, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that have observed consistent firing levels before saccade onset.

claim: There appears to be a fixed activity threshold that serves as a trigger for eye movements.
source: That is, there appears to be a fixed activity threshold that serves as a trigger for eye movements (Lo and Wang, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study that proposed a fixed activity threshold for triggering eye movements.

claim: It is widely thought that, for simple saccades to lone, unambiguous stimuli, the variance of the RT distribution is predominantly determined by the variance of the FEF/SC build-up rates across trials.
source: Thus, it is widely thought that, for simple saccades to lone, unambiguous stimuli, i.e., reactive saccades, the variance of the RT distribution is predominantly determined by the variance of the FEF/SC build-up rates across trials (Carpenter and Williams, 1995; Hanes and Schall, 1996; Fecteau and Munoz, 2007; Sumner, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that support this widely held view.

claim: The preparation to make a saccade of a particular direction and amplitude is equal to a gradual rise in the activity of oculomotor neurons that are selective for the corresponding movement vector.
source: In essence, the preparation to make a saccade of a particular direction and amplitude is equal to a gradual rise in the activity of oculomotor neurons that are selective for the corresponding movement vector.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in the field of oculomotor control, based on extensive prior research.

claim: If the rising activity (motor plan) ramps up rapidly, the saccade is initiated quickly; if the motor plan grows more slowly, the saccade starts later.
source: If this rising activity, referred to as a motor plan, ramps up rapidly, the saccade is initiated quickly; if the motor plan grows more slowly, the saccade starts later.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the rise-to-threshold mechanism and is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: There is a negative correlation between saccadic RT and build-up rate.
source: Quantitatively, this corresponds to a negative correlation between saccadic RT and build-up rate (Hanes and Schall, 1996; Fecteau and Munoz, 2007; Ding and Gold, 2012; Heitz and Schall, 2012; Costello et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that have documented this negative correlation.

claim: When trials were sorted by bias and outcome, the simulated neural responses reproduced the covariations in baseline, build-up rate, and threshold across conditions.
source: With all of these elements in place, the model parameters were adjusted to fit all of the experimental data discussed so far ('Materials and methods, Correspondence between data and model parameters'). In this way, when trials were sorted by bias and outcome, the simulated neural responses reproduced the covariations in baseline, build-up rate, and threshold across conditions (Figure 5d–f; for quantification, see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports that the model reproduced the observed covariations, as shown in Figure 5d-f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: When RTs are not matched, the responses in III and IOI trials differ patently in baseline, threshold, and build-up rate.
source: Qualitatively, the results are just as expected from the model: when the RTs are not matched, the responses in III and IOI trials differ patently in baseline, threshold, and build-up rate (Figure 6e), and the corresponding curves intersect each other twice when the spikes are aligned on saccade onset (right panel).
evidence: The manuscript reports the observed differences in neural responses when RTs are not matched, as shown in Figure 6e.

claim: When RTs are matched between III and IOI trials, the differences in build-up rate practically disappear, and those in baseline and threshold become smaller.
source: In contrast, when the RTs are matched, the differences in build-up rate practically disappear, and those in baseline and threshold become smaller (Figure 6f).
evidence: The manuscript reports the observed changes in neural responses when RTs are matched, as shown in Figure 6f.

claim: The results of RT matching were qualitatively similar across FEF cell categories (V, VM, and M).
source: These results were qualitatively similar across FEF cell categories (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states that the RT matching results were similar across cell types, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: With the parameter adjustments for ADR, the model generated less extreme variations in baseline, build-up rate, and threshold, and was able to replicate both the neural activity and the RT distribution measured in ADR trials.
source: With those changes, the model generated less extreme variations in baseline, build-up rate, and threshold, and was able to replicate both the neural activity and the RT distribution measured in ADR trials (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports that the model successfully reproduced ADR data, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The sensitivity to RT spanned a similar range for all elements of the FEF circuitry (V, VM, M, and other cell types).
source: So, as far as we could tell, the sensitivity to RT spanned a similar range for all the elements of the FEF circuitry.
evidence: The manuscript infers from the statistical analysis that RT sensitivity is similar across cell types.

claim: The moderate RT sensitivity seen in the average population activity during IOI trials is the sum of two opposing contributions from subpopulations with temporal preferences that partially offset each other.
source: These results explain the moderate RT sensitivity seen in the average population activity during IOI trials (Figure 7e) as the sum of two opposing contributions from subpopulations with temporal preferences that partially offset each other.
evidence: The manuscript infers this explanation from the analysis of subpopulations with different RT preferences.

claim: The two components of target-driven activity (RU and RC) correspond to the two neuronal types with opposite RT preferences (fast-preferring and slow-preferring).
source: These two components correspond to the two neuronal types with opposite RT preferences.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the correspondence between model components and observed neuronal types.

claim: According to the model, the variability of the initial build-up rate is the fundamental mechanistic distinction between the fast- and slow-preferring FEF neurons.
source: According to the model, this feature, the variability of the initial build-up rate, is the fundamental mechanistic distinction between the fast- and slow-preferring FEF neurons.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanistic explanation based on the model's structure and behavior.

claim: The large variance in RT observed during incongruent trials vastly exceeds that associated with intrinsic noise in the rising activity, and is fundamentally determined by the covert conflict between competing saccade plans and the ensuing dynamics.
source: Nevertheless, the conclusion is clear: the large variance in RT observed during incongruent trials vastly exceeds that associated with intrinsic noise in the rising activity, and is fundamentally determined by the covert conflict between competing saccade plans and the ensuing dynamics; whereas the much smaller variance in RT observed during congruent trials is best explained by noise that is independent of the competitive interactions, which make just a modest contribution in that case.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the model analysis and comparison with experimental data.

claim: The much smaller variance in RT observed during congruent trials is best explained by noise that is independent of the competitive interactions.
source: Nevertheless, the conclusion is clear: the large variance in RT observed during incongruent trials vastly exceeds that associated with intrinsic noise in the rising activity, and is fundamentally determined by the covert conflict between competing saccade plans and the ensuing dynamics; whereas the much smaller variance in RT observed during congruent trials is best explained by noise that is independent of the competitive interactions, which make just a modest contribution in that case.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the model analysis and comparison with experimental data.

claim: FEF is a cortical area whose role in saccade generation and attentional deployment is firmly established.
source: We examined single-neuron activity in FEF, a cortical area whose role in saccade generation and attentional deployment is firmly established (Bruce and Goldberg, 1985; Tehovnik et al., 2000; Squire et al., 2012), and where the activity of movement-related neurons is perhaps most emblematic of the idealized rise to threshold (Hanes and Schall, 1996; Fecteau and Munoz, 2007; Stanford et al., 2010; Ding and Gold, 2012; Costello et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that have established FEF's role in saccade generation and attention.

claim: The activity of movement-related neurons in FEF is perhaps most emblematic of the idealized rise to threshold.
source: We examined single-neuron activity in FEF, a cortical area whose role in saccade generation and attentional deployment is firmly established (Bruce and Goldberg, 1985; Tehovnik et al., 2000; Squire et al., 2012), and where the activity of movement-related neurons is perhaps most emblematic of the idealized rise to threshold (Hanes and Schall, 1996; Fecteau and Munoz, 2007; Stanford et al., 2010; Ding and Gold, 2012; Costello et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that have characterized FEF activity as exemplifying the rise-to-threshold process.

claim: The baseline activity, build-up rate, and threshold of the rise-to-threshold process fluctuate in a coordinated fashion.
source: We found that the three main components of this process — the baseline activity preceding target presentation, the build-up rate of the evoked response, and the saccade threshold — fluctuate in a coordinated fashion.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the analysis of FEF neuronal data.

claim: The high variance in RT results not from noisy representations or sloppy computations, but rather from the normal operation of a motor-selection machine.
source: Thus, the high variance in RT results not from noisy representations or sloppy computations, but rather from the normal operation of a well-oiled motor-selection machine (Najemnik and Geisler, 2005; Oostwoud Wijdenes et al., 2016; Tian et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the study's findings and cites related work.

claim: Noise in the build-up rate was discernible but only during congruent trials, when the target-driven activity typically starts with the higher baseline and there is minimal motor ambiguity.
source: Contrary to current ideas, we found that noise in the build-up rate is not the main source of RT variance. Such noise was discernible but only during congruent trials, when the target-driven activity typically starts with the higher baseline and there is minimal motor ambiguity to begin with (Figure 3a).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the analysis of FEF data and model simulations, as shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The proportion of variance in RT due to intrinsic randomness in build-up rate is smaller in the ADR task and may become negligible in the 1DR task incongruent trials as motor conflict increases.
source: More typically, the proportion of variance in RT due to such intrinsic randomness is smaller (ADR task), and may become negligible (1DR task, incongruent trials) as motor conflict increases.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the model analysis and comparison with experimental data across different task conditions.

claim: Critical dynamical interactions between competing motor plans may occur at quite low levels of activity, where they are less readily apparent and much more difficult to characterize without prior knowledge of their signature features.
source: This is a major departure from standard choice models, in which the outcome is not determined until activity is close to or at threshold. It means that critical dynamical interactions may occur at quite low levels of activity, where they are less readily apparent and much more difficult to characterize without prior knowledge of their signature features.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the model's behavior and its implications for understanding motor selection.

claim: Movement-related activity preceding memory-guided saccades, anti-saccades, or saccades triggered by blinks is considerably weaker than that for stimulus-driven saccades.
source: For instance, in the model, a stronger internally driven activity promotes a lower threshold, and indeed, movement-related activity preceding memory-guided saccades, anti-saccades, or saccades triggered by blinks is considerably weaker than that for stimulus-driven saccades (Edelman and Goldberg, 2001; Jantz et al., 2013; Jagadisan and Gandhi, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies that have documented weaker presaccadic activity for internally driven saccades.

claim: During visual search, the presaccadic activity measured is less vigorous for incorrect than for correct responses to the same location.
source: In addition, the presaccadic activity measured during visual search is less vigorous for incorrect than for correct responses to the same location (Thompson et al., 2005), presumably because the former involve a stronger internal (and erroneous) drive that promotes a lower threshold, just as in our data.
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study that documented this difference in presaccadic activity during visual search.

claim: During visual search, when the mean RT was shorter, the baseline, build-up rate, and threshold were all higher.
source: And, again in the context of visual search, one study (Heitz and Schall, 2012) showed multiple differences in FEF activity across task conditions similar to those found here; that is, when the mean RT was shorter, the baseline, build-up rate, and threshold were all higher.
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study that documented coordinated changes in baseline, build-up rate, and threshold during visual search.

claim: A popular idea is that adjustments in threshold may serve to trade speed against accuracy during choices.
source: For instance, a popular idea is that adjustments in threshold may serve to trade speed against accuracy during choices (Lo and Wang, 2006; Bogacz et al., 2010; Heitz and Schall, 2012; but see Salinas et al., 2014; Thura et al., 2014; Thura and Cisek, 2016, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that have proposed this idea, as well as some that have challenged it.

claim: In the 1DR task, congruent trials produce shorter RTs and higher accuracy than incongruent ones.
source: However, the results in the 1DR task are entirely antithetical to these notions: first, congruent trials produce shorter RTs and higher accuracy than incongruent ones, and second, the observed variations in threshold are linked to variations in baseline and build-up rate in ways that, according to the standard characterization of the speed-accuracy tradeoff, are entirely inconsistent.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the experimental data.

claim: The observed variations in threshold are linked to variations in baseline and build-up rate in ways that are inconsistent with the standard characterization of the speed-accuracy tradeoff.
source: However, the results in the 1DR task are entirely antithetical to these notions: first, congruent trials produce shorter RTs and higher accuracy than incongruent ones, and second, the observed variations in threshold are linked to variations in baseline and build-up rate in ways that, according to the standard characterization of the speed-accuracy tradeoff, are entirely inconsistent.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the analysis of the experimental data in relation to existing theories.

claim: A higher threshold, which lengthens the deliberation period, is typically accompanied by a higher baseline and a higher build-up rate, both of which shorten that period.
source: A higher threshold, which lengthens the deliberation period, is typically accompanied by a higher baseline and a higher build-up rate, both of which shorten that period.
evidence: The manuscript describes this observed pattern from the experimental data.

claim: The strongest evidence of a threshold's existence is the behavior of oculomotor neurons in FEF and SC.
source: These considerations are significant because, although the threshold is a universal feature of decision-making models, the strongest evidence of its existence is precisely the behavior of oculomotor neurons in FEF and SC (Hanes and Schall, 1996; Lo and Wang, 2006; Brown et al., 2008; Stanford et al., 2010; Ding and Gold, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that have provided evidence for a threshold in FEF and SC neurons.

claim: In other related circuits, either no threshold is apparent or its implementation is much less evident.
source: In other related circuits, either no threshold is apparent (Ding and Gold, 2010; Stuphorn et al., 2010) or its implementation is much less evident (Afshar et al., 2011; Hayden et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies that have examined threshold-like behavior in other brain circuits.

claim: It is well established that Gaussian variability in the build-up rate of a rise-to-threshold process accurately reproduces the characteristic skewed shapes of RT distributions.
source: Sumner (2011) has pinpointed why explaining saccadic latency distributions has been so challenging: it is well established that Gaussian variability in the build-up rate of a rise-to-threshold process accurately reproduces their characteristic skewed shapes (Carpenter and Williams, 1995; Hanes and Schall, 1996; Fecteau and Munoz, 2007), but most factors that are known to affect saccadic RT in simple tasks are normally modeled as baseline shifts (Sumner, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that have established this relationship.

claim: Most factors that are known to affect saccadic RT in simple tasks are normally modeled as baseline shifts.
source: Sumner (2011) has pinpointed why explaining saccadic latency distributions has been so challenging: it is well established that Gaussian variability in the build-up rate of a rise-to-threshold process accurately reproduces their characteristic skewed shapes (Carpenter and Williams, 1995; Hanes and Schall, 1996; Fecteau and Munoz, 2007), but most factors that are known to affect saccadic RT in simple tasks are normally modeled as baseline shifts (Sumner, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study that has identified this modeling approach.

claim: According to the model, the major source of randomness across trials is the variability of the baselines.
source: According to the model, the major source of randomness across trials is the variability of the baselines (Equation 5).
evidence: The manuscript describes this feature of the computational model.

claim: Other sources of variability, such as variations in response onset, are likely to contribute to RT variance but are likely to be very small in comparison to baseline fluctuations.
source: This is a simplification, of course. First, it is possible that the link is not strictly causal, that is, that an unidentified factor drives the fluctuations in baseline and in the other dynamic variables. And second, other sources of variability are likely to contribute too; for instance, variations in response onset (Pouget et al., 2011; Peel et al., 2017), which would correspond to fluctuations in the afferent delays of the model. These contributions, however, are likely to be very small in comparison (Pouget et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies and acknowledges other potential sources of variability while arguing they are small.

claim: The baselines reflect multiple cognitive elements, including expectation, anticipation, and the allocation of attention and other resources.
source: Arguably, the baselines reflect multiple cognitive elements, including expectation, anticipation, and the allocation of attention and other resources (Bruce and Goldberg, 1985; Kastner et al., 1999; Coe et al., 2002; Maunsell, 2004; Rao et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2014; Thura and Cisek, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that have linked baseline activity to various cognitive processes.

claim: In the model, the baseline values set the initial spatial priorities such that the neurons with the higher baseline have a higher probability of triggering the next saccade.
source: In the model, these elements set the initial spatial priorities such that the neurons with the higher baseline have a higher probability of triggering the next saccade.
evidence: The manuscript describes how baseline values function in the computational model.

claim: The effect of baseline on saccade probability is in agreement with the findings of other single-neuron studies.
source: This probability is a complicated function of the baseline values and the upcoming stimulus, but qualitatively, the effect is very much in agreement with the findings of other single-neuron studies (Everling et al., 1998; Everling and Munoz, 2000) and with the results of subthreshold microstimulation experiments (Glimcher and Sparks, 1993; Dorris et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies that have documented similar effects of baseline activity on saccade probability.

claim: The background activity in recurrent circuits can have profound dynamical and amplification effects on evoked responses.
source: It is also in line with theoretical studies showing that the background activity in recurrent circuits can have profound dynamical and amplification effects on evoked responses (Salinas and Abbott, 1996; Chance et al., 2002; Salinas, 2003; York and van Rossum, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior theoretical studies that have demonstrated this principle.

claim: Mounting evidence demonstrates that in motor cortex, the initial neural state is predictive of an ensuing arm movement and of the trajectories of the underlying neural signals over time.
source: The model proposes a tight relationship between initial state and subsequent oculomotor dynamics, and interestingly, mounting evidence demonstrates a similar phenomenon in motor cortex, whereby the initial neural state is predictive of an ensuing arm movement and of the trajectories of the underlying neural signals over time (Churchland et al., 2006, 2010, 2012; Afshar et al., 2011; Ames et al., 2014; Sheahan et al., 2016; Stavisky et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that have documented this phenomenon in motor cortex.

claim: In motor cortex, the dynamics develop within a very high-dimensional space, such that the preparatory activity is only weakly related to specific kinematic parameters.
source: In that case, the dynamics develop within a very high-dimensional space, such that the preparatory activity is only weakly related to specific kinematic parameters (Churchland et al., 2006, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies that have characterized the high-dimensional nature of motor cortex dynamics.

claim: Saccades are simpler than arm movements because they are lower dimensional and largely stereotyped, and because the activity of any given cell generally corresponds to a fixed movement vector.
source: Saccades are simpler because they are lower dimensional and largely stereotyped, and because the activity of any given cell generally corresponds to a fixed movement vector.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the properties of saccades and saccade-related neurons.

claim: The initial state of the oculomotor system (the configuration of baseline levels across RFs during fixation) fundamentally determines its subsequent temporal evolution, including its interaction with new incoming sensory information and the eventual outcome.
source: However, we propose that their dynamical behavior is qualitatively similar in that the initial state of the system — that is, the configuration of baseline levels across RFs during fixation — fundamentally determines its subsequent temporal evolution, including its interaction with new incoming sensory information (Sheahan et al., 2016) and the eventual outcome (Churchland et al., 2006; Afshar et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this similarity and cites prior studies that have documented related phenomena in motor cortex.

claim: When oculomotor circuits receive new visual information, ongoing saccade plans and internal settings radically shape the impact of that information, even when it is behaviorally relevant, expected, and unambiguous.
source: Overall, the current results suggest that, when oculomotor circuits receive new visual information, ongoing saccade plans and internal settings (e.g., threshold level and attentional locus) radically shape the impact of that information, even when it is behaviorally relevant, expected, and unambiguous.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Two adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) were used as experimental subjects.
source: Experimental subjects were two adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the species and number of subjects used.

claim: All experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, USDA regulations, and the policies set forth by the IACUC of Wake Forest School of Medicine.
source: All experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, USDA regulations, and the policies set forth by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Wake Forest School of Medicine.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the ethical guidelines followed.

claim: In the 1DR task, the fixation period was 1000 ms.
source: In the 1DR task (Figure 1a), all trials began with the appearance of a centrally located stimulus. Monkeys had to maintain their gaze on this fixation spot for 1000 ms.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the task parameters.

claim: In the 1DR task, the disappearance of the fixation spot (go signal) was simultaneous with the appearance of the target stimulus.
source: The disappearance of the fixation spot (go signal) was simultaneous with the appearance of a second, target stimulus in one of four possible locations (Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the task parameters.

claim: In the 1DR task, subjects were required to make a saccade to the peripheral target within 500 ms of the go signal in order to receive a liquid reward.
source: Subjects were required to make a saccade to the peripheral target within 500 ms of the go signal in order to receive a liquid reward.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the task requirements.

claim: In the 1DR task, target locations varied pseudorandomly from trial to trial.
source: Target locations varied pseudorandomly from trial to trial.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the task design.

claim: In the 1DR task, in each block of trials, only one of the four target locations was associated with a large reward.
source: In each block of trials, only one of the four target locations was associated with a large reward; the other three were unrewarded (Monkey G), or yielded a much smaller reward (Monkey K).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the reward structure of the task.

claim: In the 1DR task, the rewarded location changed pseudorandomly from one block to another.
source: The rewarded location changed pseudorandomly from one block to another.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the task design.

claim: In the 1DR task, block length was highly variable (range: 10–140 trials) with an average of 70 trials per block.
source: Block length was highly variable (range: 10–140 trials); the average was 70 trials per block.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the task design parameters.

claim: In the ADR task, the events were the same as in the 1DR task, but the four target locations were rewarded equally.
source: In the all-directions-rewarded task (ADR), the events were the same as in the 1DR, but the four target locations were rewarded equally (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the ADR task design.

claim: Blocks of ADR trials were run sporadically, interleaved with those of 1DR trials.
source: Blocks of ADR trials were run sporadically, interleaved with those of 1DR trials.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes how ADR trials were administered.

claim: For all analyses not specifically examining sequential effects and block transitions, the first 8 trials of each 1DR block were discarded.
source: For all analyses not specifically examining sequential effects and block transitions, we discarded the first 8 trials of each 1DR block, during which the monkeys may have been discovering the new rewarded location (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the trial exclusion criterion.

claim: To produce population responses, the continuous traces of individual cells were first normalized by each neuron's overall maximum firing rate and were then averaged across neurons.
source: To produce equivalent population responses (e.g., Figure 3a–c), the continuous traces of individual cells were first normalized by each neuron's overall maximum firing rate and were then averaged across neurons.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the method for generating population responses.

claim: Two of the 92 neurons with standard visuomotor properties lacked well-defined RFs and were excluded from the population averages.
source: Two of the 92 neurons with standard visuomotor properties lacked well-defined RFs and were excluded from the population averages.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the exclusion criterion and number of excluded neurons.

claim: Of the remaining 90 units with standard visuomotor properties, only the 62 that had error trials (IOO, OII) were considered for comparisons between correct and incorrect responses.
source: Of the remaining 90 units, only the 62 that had error trials (IOO, OII) were considered for comparisons between correct and incorrect responses (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the selection criterion for neurons used in correct vs. incorrect comparisons.

claim: All 22 model parameters were adjusted to satisfy 23 basic experimental constraints.
source: In all, 22 model parameters were adjusted to satisfy 23 basic experimental constraints: six baseline and six threshold values across conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), two error rates, and three RT distributions (Figure 5g–i), each of which requires, at a minimum, three parameters to be characterized.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the number of parameters and constraints used in model fitting.

claim: The model accounted for many more features (degrees of freedom) in the data than the 23 basic experimental constraints, pertaining to the specific shapes of response trajectories, the effect of RT equalization, the correlation between firing activity and RT before and after target onset, and the response heterogeneity across individual FEF neurons.
source: But note that the model accounted for many more features (i.e., degrees of freedom) in the data, pertaining to the specific shapes of response trajectories, the effect of RT equalization, the correlation between firing activity and RT before and after target onset, and the response heterogeneity across individual FEF neurons.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the model explained more features than the number of constraints used in fitting.
